# Module 1: The Mixed-Effects Framework {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Three Questions Before Fitting Any Model

- **What does your data structure require?** Are observations nested inside units, crossed across multiple grouping factors, or nested at three levels — and does your model reflect that structure?
- **What goes wrong without the right model?** Standard errors that are too small, fixed-effect estimates that conflate within-unit change with between-unit sorting, and predictions that cannot generalize to new units.
- **What does each step add — and what does it cost?** Moving from pooled OLS to fixed effects to random intercepts to random slopes imposes progressively stronger distributional assumptions. Each model buys something new and requires something new in return.
:::

## The Toolkit

Module 0 established that your data is almost always nested and that ignoring nesting inflates Type I error, shrinks effective sample sizes, and obscures the true data-generating process. Now we build the tools to do something about it.

The **mixed-effects model** is the central workhorse of nested data analysis. It is called "mixed" because it combines two types of effects:

- **Fixed effects** — parameters that apply to the entire population. The average relationship between sleep and mood. The overall effect of a treatment.
- **Random effects** — parameters that vary across units (people, firms, classrooms) and are treated as drawn from a distribution rather than estimated individually.

This combination lets the model do something powerful: borrow strength across units. A student who was absent for half the year still contributes information about their classroom. A person who completed only 2 days of a diary still informs estimates of the group average. The model uses all available information, weighted by how much each unit tells us.

## How This Module is Organized

The module builds in steps, each adding one layer of complexity while being explicit about what assumption is being made and what assumption is being relaxed.

**Part 1: Fixed Effects** introduces the fixed-effects estimator — the simplest approach to handling nesting. It is easy to understand and makes strong assumptions. We examine each assumption carefully and show when it fails.

**Part 2: Random Intercepts** introduces the random-intercept mixed model: the most common multilevel model in psychology. We show how it differs from fixed effects, what it assumes, and how to check those assumptions.

**Part 3: Random Slopes** adds the most important extension: allowing the relationship between a predictor and outcome to vary across units. We discuss when this matters and when it does not.

**Part 4: Fixed vs. Random — When to Use Which** addresses one of the most frequently asked questions in applied multilevel analysis. The answer involves the scientific question, the data structure, and several testable assumptions.

**Part 5: Three-Level Structures** extends the framework to three levels of nesting and introduces the challenge of variance decomposition across levels.

**Part 6: Crossed Random Effects** covers the case where observations belong to multiple grouping factors simultaneously — the structure that arises naturally in most psychological experiments.

## The Model Family at a Glance

Before diving into each part, here is a map of the model family this module builds — what each step buys you, and — critically — what it still does not give you.

| Problem in your data | Model move | What it buys you | What it does **not** buy you |
|---|---|---|---|
| Repeated observations within a unit | Random intercept | Corrects standard errors for dependence in levels | Causal identification of predictors |
| Effect of X differs across units | Random slope | Models heterogeneity in the X–Y relationship | Does not solve confounding of X |
| Stable unit-level confounding | Fixed effects | Removes time-invariant omitted variables | Does not remove time-varying confounding |
| Participants *and* stimuli both sampled | Crossed random effects | Generalizes inference across both sources of sampling | Does not fix design flaws or demand effects |
| Units nested in higher units | Three-level model | Partitions variance correctly; avoids pseudo-replication | Does not identify causal pathways across levels |

: Model family overview. The last column is what drives Module 3. {tbl-colwidths="[22,20,30,28]"}

```{r assumption-map, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.width=10}
#| fig-cap: "Assumption burden and capability across model families. Green = advantage or assumption not needed; Amber = assumption you must meet; Red = limitation or violated by design; Grey = not applicable."
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

models <- c("Pooled\nOLS", "Fixed\nEffects", "Random\nIntercepts", "Random\nSlopes", "Crossed\nRE")

df_map <- tribble(
  ~assumption,                         ~model,             ~status,          ~label,
  "RE ⊥ X\n(no stable confound)",      "Pooled\nOLS",       "violated",       "Violated",
  "RE ⊥ X\n(no stable confound)",      "Fixed\nEffects",    "not_needed",     "Not needed",
  "RE ⊥ X\n(no stable confound)",      "Random\nIntercepts","required_star",  "Required ★",
  "RE ⊥ X\n(no stable confound)",      "Random\nSlopes",    "required_star",  "Required ★",
  "RE ⊥ X\n(no stable confound)",      "Crossed\nRE",       "required_star",  "Required ★",
  "Normality of\nrandom effects",       "Pooled\nOLS",       "not_applicable", "N/A",
  "Normality of\nrandom effects",       "Fixed\nEffects",    "not_applicable", "N/A",
  "Normality of\nrandom effects",       "Random\nIntercepts","required",       "Required",
  "Normality of\nrandom effects",       "Random\nSlopes",    "required",       "Required",
  "Normality of\nrandom effects",       "Crossed\nRE",       "required",       "Required",
  "Between-unit variance\nhandling",    "Pooled\nOLS",       "violated",       "Confounded",
  "Between-unit variance\nhandling",    "Fixed\nEffects",    "benefit",        "Removed",
  "Between-unit variance\nhandling",    "Random\nIntercepts","benefit",        "Estimated",
  "Between-unit variance\nhandling",    "Random\nSlopes",    "benefit",        "Estimated",
  "Between-unit variance\nhandling",    "Crossed\nRE",       "benefit",        "Both estimated",
  "Heterogeneous\nslopes",              "Pooled\nOLS",       "violated",       "Ignored",
  "Heterogeneous\nslopes",              "Fixed\nEffects",    "violated",       "Ignored",
  "Heterogeneous\nslopes",             "Random\nIntercepts","violated",       "Ignored",
  "Heterogeneous\nslopes",              "Random\nSlopes",    "benefit",        "Modeled",
  "Heterogeneous\nslopes",              "Crossed\nRE",       "partial",        "Partial",
  "Generalise to\nnew units",           "Pooled\nOLS",       "partial",        "Yes (naive)",
  "Generalise to\nnew units",           "Fixed\nEffects",    "violated",       "No",
  "Generalise to\nnew units",           "Random\nIntercepts","benefit",        "Yes",
  "Generalise to\nnew units",           "Random\nSlopes",    "benefit",        "Yes",
  "Generalise to\nnew units",           "Crossed\nRE",       "benefit",        "Yes"
) |>
  mutate(
    model = factor(model, levels = models),
    assumption = factor(assumption, levels = rev(c(
      "RE ⊥ X\n(no stable confound)",
      "Normality of\nrandom effects",
      "Between-unit variance\nhandling",
      "Heterogeneous\nslopes",
      "Generalise to\nnew units"
    )))
  )

status_colors <- c(
  "violated"       = "#f4a7a3",
  "not_needed"     = "#b7e4c7",
  "required_star"  = "#fdd9a0",
  "required"       = "#fdd9a0",
  "benefit"        = "#b7e4c7",
  "not_applicable" = "#e8e8e8",
  "partial"        = "#dde9f7"
)

ggplot(df_map, aes(x = model, y = assumption, fill = status, label = label)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.9, width = 0.95, height = 0.92) +
  geom_text(size = 2.9, lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = status_colors, guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title    = "Assumption burden and capability across model families",
    subtitle = "Green = advantage or not needed  |  Amber = required assumption  |  Red = concern  |  Grey = N/A\n★ = the key assumption that distinguishes random effects from fixed effects",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid  = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9)
  )
```

The rightmost column is intentional. Every model in this module corrects a **dependence problem** — observations that are not independent. None of them, on their own, solve an **identification problem** — the question of whether your predictor is truly exogenous. That distinction is the heart of Module 3.

## Core Assumptions

Every model in this module makes assumptions. We will state them explicitly at each step. For now, here is the set of assumptions that span the entire module:

::: {.callout-important icon=false}
## Assumptions of the Mixed-Effects Framework

1. **Linearity:** The relationship between predictors and the outcome is linear (at each level)
2. **Normality of random effects:** The random effects are drawn from a normal distribution
3. **Normality of residuals:** Level-1 residuals are normally distributed
4. **Homoskedasticity:** The variance of residuals is constant across units and predictor values
5. **Independence of residuals:** Level-1 residuals are independent *after* conditioning on the random effects
6. **Independence of random effects from predictors:** (for random effects models) The random effects are uncorrelated with the fixed-effect predictors

Not all of these apply to all models. Fixed-effects models, for instance, do not require Assumption 6. Understanding *which* assumptions apply to *which* model — and how to check each one — is the goal of this module.
:::
